modules.name: Irving Fisher
modules.outcome: Describe the trade-off between spending now and investing for later, and set the saving rule you will follow.
modules.intro: Irving Fisher built his theory of interest on one question: why do people accept less now than they could get later? His answer, impatience to spend against the opportunity to invest, is the core of this module.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read the opening chapter and passages from chapters 6 and 7 of Fisher's The Rate of Interest (1907). Its first chapter says the rate of interest in any community is an index of the preference, in that community, for a dollar of present over a dollar of future income. {{lec-fisher-1907}}

He calls this time-preference and says it depends on income. People adjust the time-shape of their income, by borrowing or lending, until their own rate of preference matches the market rate of interest. {{lec-fisher-1907}}

His 1930 book, The Theory of Interest, carries the subtitle 'as determined by impatience to spend income and opportunity to invest it'. {{lec-fisher-1930cat}} The scan is access-restricted, so we did not read the book itself.
His method, step by step

i: Ask how much you value spending now against spending later. {{lec-fisher-1907}}
Compare that with the return you could earn by investing. {{lec-mh-beginners}}
Keep your emergency fund first, because it removes the need to spend investments in a crisis. {{lec-mh-beginners}}
Decide the time you can leave money untouched, and invest only what you will not need in that time.

Our inference: the £2,000 is a candidate for investing; the £6,000 stays as a safety net.

blocks.q: In Fisher's account, what sets the interest rate?
o: Impatience to spend and the opportunity to invest
blocks.w: The 1930 title names impatience to spend income and opportunity to invest it, and the 1907 book ties the rate to the preference for present over future income. {{lec-fisher-1930cat}} {{lec-fisher-1907}}

blocks.q: Fisher linked interest to two things. One is impatience to spend; what is the other?
blocks.w: The 1930 title names impatience to spend income and opportunity to invest it. {{lec-fisher-1930cat}}

i: Time-preference depends on income, so how much you need now should set how much you invest (our inference). {{lec-fisher-1907}}
Build the emergency fund before investing. {{lec-mh-beginners}}

modules.name: Irving Fisher
modules.outcome: Compare the value of a sum over time, and separate the real return from the nominal one.
modules.intro: Fisher thought in present and future values as a matter of course. This lesson uses his habit of comparing money across time.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

In The Rate of Interest, Fisher shows that a change in the rate changes the income streams people choose: a high rate favours quickly returning incomes, and a low rate favours distant returns. {{lec-fisher-1907}}
He also notes that the value of capital sinks as the rate of interest rises, if the income from the capital stays the same. {{lec-fisher-1907}}
We use the compound-growth arithmetic from module 2, which is our own calculation, not a quotation.
His method, step by step

i: Write the present sum and the rate, and decide the number of years.
Calculate the future value with the factor of one plus the rate, raised to the years. Our arithmetic.
Adjust the rate for inflation, to see the real figure. {{lec-mh-beginners}}
Compare the result with a different rate or time, and note what changed.

modules.name: Louis Bachelier
modules.outcome: Explain the random walk, and why a plan should cover a range of outcomes.
modules.intro: Bachelier wrote in 1900 about the theory of speculation and modelled prices as a random walk. His idea still shapes how investors think about short-term moves.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

Bachelier's 1900 thesis, Théorie de la spéculation, begins by saying that the influences on prices are countless, so a mathematical forecast of their movements is impossible, and that the calculus of probabilities will probably never apply to the movements of quoted prices. {{lec-bachelier-1900}}

What he sets out to find is the probability law of price changes that the market allows at a given moment, since a market that does not predict movements still treats some as more probable than others. {{lec-bachelier-1900}}
We read the introduction and sampled later sections in French. We did not work through the mathematics.
His method, step by step

i: Accept that price movements cannot be forecast mathematically, as he begins by saying. {{lec-bachelier-1900}}
Do not judge a holding by one good or bad period.
Plan for a range of outcomes, not a single forecast. {{lec-fca-risk}}
Check that your plan still makes sense in a fall as well as in a rise.

blocks.title: What the model does and does not say
head: Claim
Status
rows: Short-term prices are hard to predict
Not what the model says; treat as a misreading
Your plan will never make money
Not implied; the point is fragility of forecasts

blocks.x: Range of outcomes (illustrative)

blocks.title: Illustrative: a £10,000 holding could be £7,000 after a bad year or £13,000 after a good one.
steps: Plan for both, and check that the fall would not force a sale.
Our inference: the plan must survive the bad end of the range.

blocks.x: Your plan's bad year

i: Choose a fall you think is plausible for your holding.
Calculate the recovery needed, using the module 3 table.
Write what you would do, and whether you could afford to wait.

blocks.x: Write the fall you would survive and the rise needed to recover from it.

blocks.q: What does the random walk suggest about a plan that depends on forecasting next month?
blocks.w: Bachelier begins from the impossibility of forecasting price movements, so a plan built on forecasts is fragile (our inference). {{lec-bachelier-1900}}

blocks.q: Which statement misreads the random walk model?
o: Short-term moves are hard to predict
Prices are pure chance, so nobody can ever do well
Plans should cover a range of outcomes
blocks.w: His starting point is that forecasting is impossible, not that outcomes are pure chance or that nobody can do well. Our reading of {{lec-bachelier-1900}}

i: Bachelier starts from the point that price movements cannot be forecast mathematically. {{lec-bachelier-1900}}
Plan for a range of outcomes, including the bad end. {{lec-fca-risk}}
The model is an idea to test, not a guarantee.

quiz.q: What does a random walk describe?
o: A path where each step is unpredictable from the last
quiz.w: That is our definition of a random walk; Bachelier's thesis begins from the impossibility of forecasting. {{lec-bachelier-1900}}

modules.name: Harry Markowitz
modules.outcome: Explain how holdings that move apart reduce portfolio risk, and write a portfolio you can defend.
modules.intro: Markowitz showed in 1952 that the risk of a portfolio depends on how its holdings move together, not only on each one alone. This lesson uses that point to check your own split.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

Markowitz's 1952 paper 'Portfolio Selection' rejects the rule of maximising expected return because it never implies diversification, and proposes instead that investors treat expected return as desirable and variance of return as undesirable. {{lec-markowitz-1952}}

He says diversification cannot eliminate all variance, because returns from securities are too intercorrelated, and that it is necessary to avoid securities with high covariances among themselves. {{lec-markowitz-1952}}
We read the argument and the diversification passages through a fetched PDF copy, not every page. His geometric figures were not worked through.
His method, step by step

i: Name the holdings in your portfolio, and say what each one depends on. {{lec-markowitz-1952}}
Ask whether two holdings are likely to fall together in a bad year.
Check that no single holding has more risk than you can bear. {{lec-fca-risk}}
Write one reason for each holding, and one trigger for changing the split.

blocks.x: Check the efficient frontier idea (illustrative)

blocks.title: Illustrative: two portfolios offer the same expected return.
steps: The one with the lower risk is nearer the frontier.
Our inference: choose the lower-risk option for the same return.

blocks.x: Review your split

i: List your holdings and their rough share of the pot.
Mark any two that tend to move together.
Note whether any single holding is too large to bear.

blocks.x: Write your holdings, the pairs that move together, and one trigger for a review.

blocks.q: In the paper, what is an efficient portfolio?
o: The one with the highest possible return
One with the lowest variance for its expected return, or the highest return for its variance
blocks.w: Efficient portfolios have the lowest variance for a given expected return, or the highest expected return for a given variance. {{lec-markowitz-1952}}

blocks.q: Two holdings that tend to fall together give you...
blocks.w: Holdings with high covariances among themselves do little to lower portfolio risk. {{lec-markowitz-1952}}

i: Risk depends on how holdings move together. {{lec-markowitz-1952}}
Avoid securities with high covariances among themselves. {{lec-markowitz-1952}}
His first statement assumed fixed beliefs and left a general treatment for later.

quiz.q: What did Markowitz's 1952 paper focus on?
o: The risk of a portfolio depending on how holdings move together
quiz.w: The paper links portfolio risk to how holdings move together. {{lec-markowitz-1952}}

modules.name: John Bogle
modules.outcome: Compare the cost of a fund with its benefit, and use the SPIVA evidence with its limits.
modules.intro: John Bogle founded Vanguard in 1974 and is credited with popularising the index fund. He argued that low costs are one of the few things an investor can control. This lesson applies that argument.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

In his own speech, Bogle says Vanguard began operations on 19/09/1974 and was incorporated on 24/09/1974, and that it formed the first index mutual fund in 1975. {{lec-bogle-2016}} Wikipedia dates the First Index Investment Trust to 1976, so the sources differ by a year. {{lec-wiki-bogle}}
In a 1997 speech he argues that costs matter. He compares a 0.2% annual cost on $10,000, which costs $280 over ten years, with 2.2%, which costs $2,810. {{lec-bogle-1997}}
In a balanced-fund study he describes, average funds fell 1.2 percentage points a year short of the index composite, and expenses accounted for 83% of that shortfall. {{lec-bogle-1997}}
The SPIVA table in module 5 gives the US evidence on active funds against an index. {{lec-spiva}}
His method, step by step

i: Find the total annual charge of each fund you consider. {{lec-mh-beginners}}
Compare it with the cost of an index tracker that covers the same market.
Ask what the active fund must do to justify its extra cost, after fees. {{lec-bogle-1997}}
Check the SPIVA evidence, remembering it is US data and not UK advice. {{lec-spiva}}

modules.name: Benjamin Graham
modules.outcome: Apply Graham's test of investment against speculation, and use a margin of safety before you buy.
modules.intro: Benjamin Graham is called the father of value investing. He insisted that investors separate analysis from hope, and that they buy with a margin of safety.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

In The Intelligent Investor, Graham repeats his 1934 definition: an investment operation, upon thorough analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate return, and operations that do not meet those requirements are speculative. {{lec-graham-ii}}

In Chapter 20 he treats the margin of safety as the central concept: to have a true investment, a true margin of safety must be present, and the concept rests on simple arithmetical reasoning from statistical data. {{lec-graham-ii}}
We read Chapter 1 and Chapter 20 passages, not the whole book.
His method, step by step

i: Ask whether the operation rests on analysis or on hope. {{lec-graham-ii}}
Estimate what the asset is worth, and write the basis for your estimate.
Buy only with a margin between your estimate and the price. {{lec-graham-ii}}
Check the firm on the FCA Firm Checker and the Warning List before any payment. {{lec-mh-scams}} {{lec-fca-scams}}

steps: Your margin is 25%, and you still have room if your estimate is 20% too high.
Our inference: the margin protects you from error, but guarantees nothing.

blocks.q: What makes an operation an investment, in Graham's test?

blocks.w: Analysis, safety of principal and an adequate return. {{lec-graham-ii}}

i: Analysis, not hope, separates investment from speculation. {{lec-graham-ii}}
A margin of safety is a cushion, not a guarantee. {{lec-graham-ii}}
Check the firm before any payment. {{lec-fca-scams}}

quiz.q: What is a margin of safety?
o: A gap between price and estimated value
quiz.w: It is the gap between price and estimated value. {{lec-graham-ii}}

modules.name: Benjamin Graham

modules.intro: Graham's last test for a plan is whether it could survive being wrong. This lesson asks you to check your capstone plan in that way.
